foods.name: Chicken breast
foods.tagline: Lean, mild and two-thirds water. Quietly the safest thing on the menu.
overview: Skinless roast chicken breast is about 31 g protein, 65 g water and under 4 g fat per 100 g, with very little sodium (USDA). It's the gym-bag staple, the sandwich filler and the thing everyone overcooks.
With almost no salt in it, the water sets the limit: about 9.7 kg of chicken breast, or roughly 45 whole cooked breasts. You'd get bored of chicken a very long way before that.

facts.label: Typical serving
facts.value: 1 single breast, edible part (213 g, NZ data) or half a breast (86 g)

foods.funFact: The global live chicken population passed 26.5 billion in 2023, with over 50 billion more slaughtered each year.

foods.name: Beef mince
foods.tagline: Dinner's workhorse, and a surprisingly big pile of water with a side of protein.
overview: Pan-cooked 85% lean beef mince is about 25 g protein, 14 g fat and 61 g water per 100 g, with only 79 mg of sodium before you season it (USDA). The salt gets added at the stove, not by the cow.
So it's water again: about 10.4 kg of cooked mince, or roughly 125 burger patties. The most dangerous thing in the pan is the spitting fat.
foods.funFact: Cooked beef mince is still about 60% water by weight (USDA: 60.6 g per 100 g), which is how water ends up as the headline.

foods.name: Pork loin
foods.tagline: Sunday roast energy, with less salt than you'd think and more water than you'd guess.
overview: Roast pork loin (lean and fat) has about 27 g protein, 15 g fat and 58 g water per 100 g, and only 59 mg of sodium, a small fraction of what bacon carries (USDA). Fresh pork isn't a salty food, however it gets treated later.
Water sets the limit again: about 11.0 kg of roast pork loin, or 129 three-ounce servings. The apple sauce would run out first.
foods.funFact: Pork loin carries just 59 mg of sodium per 100 g (USDA); NZ's database lists ham at 1,500 mg, so curing does the salting.

foods.name: Bacon
foods.tagline: Delicious, and easily the saltiest thing in this category.
overview: Pan-fried bacon is the salt champion of this list: about 2.4 g of sodium per 100 g (roughly 6 g of salt), plus 32 g protein and 28 g fat (NZ Food Composition Database). Curing and frying concentrate it all.
That sodium sets the limit: about 3.5 kg of bacon at the rat-derived dose, or roughly 410 streaky rashers. You'd run out of packet, then fridge, then supermarket.

facts.value: 1 rasher of middle or shoulder bacon (23.8 g)

facts.label: Sodium
facts.value: 2,370 mg per 100 g (about 6 g of salt)

foods.funFact: NZ's food composition database lists two rasher sizes: 8.5 g for streaky and 23.8 g for middle or shoulder bacon.

foods.name: Lamb leg
foods.form: cooked (roasted), NZ lamb leg, lean and fat
foods.tagline: The Kiwi Sunday roast: low in salt, big on water, long on leftovers.
overview: Roast New Zealand leg of lamb (lean and fat) has about 25 g protein, 16 g fat and 58 g water per 100 g, and just 43 mg of sodium (USDA's record for imported NZ lamb). The salt arrives with the gravy.
Water sets the limit: about 10.9 kg of roast lamb, or 128 servings of 85 g. Mint sauce not included.
foods.funFact: Sheep farming was New Zealand's most important agricultural industry for 130 years, until dairy overtook it in 1987.

foods.name: Egg
foods.tagline: Nature's tidy protein capsule, about three-quarters water.
overview: A hard-boiled egg is about 75% water, with 12.6 g protein and 10.6 g fat per 100 g, and 124 mg of sodium (USDA). It also carries 373 mg of cholesterol per 100 g, which is why eggs have spent decades on trial in the court of public opinion.
Water sets the limit: about 8.4 kg of boiled egg, or roughly 169 large eggs, which is 14 dozen. You'd run out of egg cups, and chickens, first.
foods.funFact: A hard-boiled egg is about three-quarters water (USDA: 74.6 g per 100 g).

foods.name: Milk
foods.tagline: A glass of mostly water, with calcium and a faint sense of childhood.
overview: Whole cow's milk is about 88% water, with 3.2 g protein, 3.3 g fat and 5 g lactose per 100 g, plus 43 mg of sodium and 132 mg of potassium (USDA). It is basically water with ambition.
Water sets the limit: about 7.1 kg of milk, or roughly 6.9 litres at 1.03 g/mL. That's a trolley of cartons and a very patient cow.

facts.label: Density
facts.value: About 1.03 g/mL (USDA: 976 g per US quart)

foods.funFact: A litre of milk weighs about 1,031 g, roughly 3% more than a litre of water (from USDA's 976 g per US quart).

foods.name: Cheddar cheese
foods.tagline: Sharp, salty, and about as far from lethal as a cheese board gets.
overview: Cheddar is about 37% water, 33 g fat and 23 g protein per 100 g, with 653 mg of sodium (USDA). Cheese needs salt for flavour, texture and keeping, which is why it makes crackers taste like something.
At the rat-derived salt dose you'd need about 12.7 kg of cheddar, which is 452 one-ounce slices. You'd run out of crackers, then friends.
foods.funFact: Cheddar is named after the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England.

foods.name: Butter (salted)
foods.tagline: Mostly fat, a bit of salt, and extremely difficult to eat in bulk.
overview: Salted butter is about 81 g fat, 16 g water and 643 mg of sodium per 100 g (USDA). Only the sodium really sets a limit, since there's hardly any potassium, and no sugar to speak of.
At the rat-derived salt dose you'd need about 12.8 kg of butter, or roughly 905 tablespoons. Your toast would be the first casualty.
foods.funFact: Butter is only about 81% fat (USDA: 81.1 g per 100 g salted); most of the rest is water, at 16.2 g.

foods.name: Yoghurt (plain, whole milk)
foods.tagline: Milk that took up a hobby: mostly water, live cultures, no ambitions.
overview: Plain whole-milk yoghurt is about 88% water, with 3.5 g protein, 3.3 g fat, 4.7 g sugars and 46 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). Bacteria turn some of the lactose into lactic acid, which is where the tang comes from.
Water sets the limit: about 7.2 kg of yoghurt, or 42 small tubs. Even the cultures would be exhausted.
foods.funFact: Yoghurt is made by two bacteria, Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, fermenting the lactose in milk.

foods.name: Salmon
foods.tagline: Oily, pink and rich in omega-3, and also about 65% water.
overview: Cooked farmed Atlantic salmon has about 22 g protein, 12 g fat and 65 g water per 100 g, with only 61 mg of sodium and 384 mg of potassium (USDA). A notable extra is vitamin D, at 13 µg per 100 g.
Water sets the limit again: about 9.7 kg of salmon, or 55 half-fillets. Potassium is high for a fish but still finishes well behind.
foods.funFact: Salmon flesh is pink-orange because of astaxanthin, a pigment from the crustaceans they eat (farmed salmon get it added to their feed).

foods.name: Tuna (canned in brine)

foods.funFact: Some tuna species, such as bluefin, can keep their bodies warmer than the water around them.

flagged.name: Beef liver (cooked, braised)
flagged.reason: Real acute and cumulative toxicity from vitamin A (preformed retinol) at ordinary serving sizes, far below anything the lab LD50 maths suggests.
flagged.details: USDA SR Legacy 168626 (braised beef liver, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/168626/nutrients): retinol 9428 µg (9.43 mg) per 100 g. A single 100 g serving is about 6.3x the 1.5 mg/day vitamin A figure the NHS gives as a daily ceiling for some groups, and the NHS advises not eating liver more than about once a week (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-a/). USDA's record for NZ-imported boiled beef liver (174728) lists 21014 µg (21.0 mg) retinol per 100 g, about 14x that figure. Lab-style lethal masses for a 70 kg person, per 100 g composition: water 10712 g (water 58.81 g per 100 g, rat oral >90 mL/kg lower bound), sodium 104566 g (79 mg per 100 g), potassium 27117 g (352 mg per 100 g), copper 58540 g (14.283 mg per 100 g; copper(II) sulfate rat oral 300 mg/kg per PubChem https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/24462, Cu = 63.546/159.602 = 39.8% of CuSO4, giving 119.4 mg Cu/kg), vitamin A 1908146 g (retinol mouse oral LD50 2570 mg/kg per PubChem https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/445354; no rat oral value found). So every lab number says 'absurd' (the smallest is water at about 10.7 kg), but that is exactly why the lab number misleads here: the real problem is vitamin A building up at serving sizes of a few hundred grams a week, not an acute LD50.

problems: Composition data: USDA values were read from the official SR Legacy bulk CSV download (FoodData_Central_sr_legacy_food_csv_2018-04.zip from https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-datasets/, records dated 2019-04-01) because the FoodData Central API's DEMO_KEY was rate-limited (HTTP 429). The 'url' on each USDA source is the FDC page for the same fdcId; I did not open those pages in a browser. The numbers are the same records.

NZ composition data (bacon, ham, prawns, tuna in brine, green-lipped mussels) were read from the NZ Food Composition Database Concise Tables 14th edition (2021) Excel file at https://www.foodcomposition.co.nz/downloads/concise-14-edition.xlsx (the online search page is JavaScript-only). NZ figures are rounded to 2 to 3 significant figures.

How I chose between USDA and NZ: USDA by default. NZ was used where USDA lacks the exact form (green-lipped mussels; tuna 'in brine, drained', where USDA only has 'in water') or where the NZ product is much saltier (bacon 2,370 vs USDA 1,684 mg Na/100 g; ham 1,500 vs 814; prawns 552 vs 111) so the more cautious, smaller-mass figure is used. Where the two agreed within about 15% (cheddar, butter, feta, sausage, milk, cream, ice cream) USDA was used and the NZ figure is mentioned in notes.
Green-lipped mussels: no swap was needed. NZ FOODfiles has 'Mussel, green, meat, boiled' (T1026), so the entry is for the actual species. USDA only has blue mussels.

WATER LD50 is a lower bound. The only source I could open that gives a rat oral value is an archived ScienceLab SDS (Wayback capture): 'LD50 Rat oral > 90 ml/kg'. PubChem has no oral value for water (only mouse intraperitoneal values, 25,000 and 190,000 mg/kg), Fisher's water SDS lists none, and ECHA/Sigma pages were blocked. So every water-based figure (12 of the 19 foods) is a floor on the lethal food mass, not a measured median. ScienceLab's site is defunct; the URL is the Wayback capture.

Potassium chloride: the only rat oral value I could open is 2600 mg/kg (Fisher SDS). PubChem lists no rat oral value, but does list a mouse oral value of 383 mg/kg (and guinea pig 2500). The mouse figure is NOT used (a rat value exists). For transparency: if it were used, potassium would become the limiting constituent for several meats, with the smallest potassium-based masses being bacon 3,340 g, pork-loin 3,446 g, salmon 3,662 g, beef-mince 4,029 g, still 'large' or 'absurd' but headline would change.

Sodium chloride: PubChem gives rat oral 3000 mg/kg and Fisher's SDS gives 3550 mg/kg; the lower 3000 is the working number. PubChem also quotes 1000 mg/kg for humans in one record, which is not a rat value and is not used.

Bacon is only just 'large' (about 3.5 kg, via sodium) and ham only just 'absurd' (about 5.5 kg). Humans react to big salt loads at lower doses than rats do, so the lab-derived mass is generous. Both pass the spec's thresholds so they are in `foods`, but you may want to downgrade or hide bacon if you want extra caution.

Calcium (as calcium chloride) was considered for the cheeses and milk but NOT included: PubChem lists only rabbit oral values for CaCl2, and the SDS pages I tried (Sigma, ECHA, guessed Fisher part numbers) were blocked or not found, so there is no sourced rat oral LD50 to use. If a rat value around 1,000 to 2,000 mg/kg exists it could make cheddar's limit lower than the sodium-based one. Not computed.

Lactose has no rat oral LD50 that I opened, so dairy sugars are left out. Ice cream uses total sugars with the sucrose LD50 (29,700 mg/kg, PubChem) as a stand-in; sucrose and water give nearly the same answer (9.8 vs 10.3 kg), so the choice barely matters.

Beef liver is in `flagged`, not `foods`, for real-world vitamin A toxicity (see details). I could not open a rat oral LD50 for vitamin A: PubChem's retinol record has a mouse oral value (2,570 mg/kg) only, used in the flagged details and labelled as mouse. Copper uses PubChem's copper(II) sulfate rat oral 300 mg/kg (the record does not say if that is anhydrous or pentahydrate; I assumed anhydrous, which is the more cautious reading).

Form notes: beef mince is USDA 85% lean / 15% fat pan-broiled patty (NZ mince is typically 10 to 20% fat). Lamb is USDA's record for imported NZ frozen leg, roasted, lean and fat. Pork loin is roasted, lean and fat. Chicken breast is roasted, meat only (no skin). Salmon is farmed Atlantic, dry-heat cooked. Cream is USDA 'heavy whipping' (about 36% fat) as the stand-in for pouring/heavy cream.

Liquids/units: milk grams per cup (244 g) and per litre (1,031 g) come from USDA's 976 g per US quart (0.9464 L), a density of about 1.03 g/mL. All masses are per 100 g, not per 100 mL. The dozen-egg unit is 12 x USDA's 50 g large egg.

I did not include extra constituents (selenium, iron, vitamin D, cholesterol, calcium, nitrite, mercury) as limiting candidates: either no sourced rat oral LD50, or their lethal masses are many times larger than water or sodium (for example, vitamin D in salmon at 13.1 µg/100 g). Nitrite in cured meats has no USDA/NZ composition value to use.

Fun facts: those with figures are from composition data above or Wikipedia (chicken population, sheep/dairy history, feta PDO, kuku/kutai, curing salt, cream whipping, yoghurt bacteria, tuna). Not independently checked against primary sources: cheddar's Somerset naming, salmon astaxanthin from feed, the 'snag'/Bunnings line. Eyeball them before publishing.
